newsitem.title: GERMANY: Europe needs a strong currency - Buba's Tietmeyer.
newsitem.headline: Europe needs a strong currency - Buba's Tietmeyer.

text.p: A united Europe needs a strong common currency to ensure the stability of the European Union and to avoid future political conflicts, Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said in a newspaper article on Saturday.

The German central bank wants the Euro to have the same stability after European Monetary Union, planned for 1999, as that already enjoyed by the deutschemark, Tietmeyer said in an article for written for Germany's Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung.

He went on to say that the Bundesbank would would enter the process of establishing the political and economic conditions for currency union with a view to securing high levels of stability for the Euro.
"Currency union must be a sustainable and stable one, with a strong currency, in order to avoid the threat of political conflict later on," Tietmeyer said.
The Bundesbank's first responsibility lay in securing the stability of the domestic currency by implementing its own monetary policies.
A stability-oriented monetary policy also helped in reaching other macroeconomic goals. A stable currency was a good foundation for growth and increased employment, Tietmeyer wrote in the article.
The Bundesbank had a watchdog role to play in the area of German monetary policy and must keep a watchful eye on developments in other sectors which could prove harmful to stability.

The Bundesbank was in a good position to act as monitor in this capacity, as it is independent of the government, and had been given a specific advisory role to the government in the federal law under which the Bundesbank was established.
This advisory role also applied to the implementation of the Maastricht criteria, which set out guidelines for countries who wish to join EMU.

However, Tietmeyer said that the Bundesbank had not been involved in setting the Maastricht criteria for budgetary deficit at three percent of GDP and for fixing national debt levels at 60 percent of GDP.

"Both of these levels, which from the Bundesbank's point of view were chosen as too generous rather than too narrow for most countries, were not introduced by the German delegations, but by others at the negotiations, as far as I am aware," Tietmeyer said.

The stability pact agreed recently by European finance ministers in Dublin had nothing to do with attempts by Germany to achieve dominance, Tietmeyer said, but was aimed at reducing the risk of potential conflict in the areas of monetary and fiscal policy.
The Bundesbank would remain committed to stability, Tietmeyer said, as this commitment had undoubtedly done more good than harm so far, in both Germany and in Europe as a whole.
